source.title: Measuring Monosemanticity in Sparse Autoencoders via Latent Activation Coherence

page_placements.theme: SAE latent monosemanticity depends on activation range, scoring metric and evaluation harness

record.file_problem: Full paper and appendices are present. Some figures and tables are flattened in the text, but the study is readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how alternative measures of monosemanticity score SAE latents, including the effect of encoder geometry; it does not reproduce the original individual-neuron analysis.
record.gate_note: The study measures coherence and monosemanticity scores for SAE latents trained on vision and vision-language model features, rather than testing the cited InceptionV1 neuron or measuring the fraction of ordinary network neurons that are polysemantic. Its MS/TMS comparisons and qualitative examples bear on measurement dependence (V7). The probe-based deletion correlations concern functional relevance, not whether individual neurons have unrelated meanings; these are recorded under fits_no_version. Anisotropy statistics and SAE/probe accuracy results are not rows because they do not themselves measure monosemanticity.
record.test_reason: The study proposes a new score (TMS) for SAE latents and compares it with embedding-based MS on SAEs trained over DINOv3, CLIP and BLIP2 features. Polysemanticity is only the motivation; no rate or degree of polysemanticity in ordinary network neurons is reported. The units scored are SAE dictionary latents, not the network neurons any version names. Its main results compare its own metric with another (TMS vs MS), so they are not tests of V7. The finding that MS depends on encoder anisotropy is a measurement-dependence result about SAE latents. It is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that TMS, a label- and encoder-free coherence score for binarized SAE latents, is less affected by encoder anisotropy than MS. It stays correlated with MS and with within-set variance, reveals differing SAE training dynamics across base models, and better predicts concept-deletion effectiveness under anisotropy (CLIP) while being competitive otherwise.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces TMS, based on pairwise Jaccard/Tversky similarity of binarized SAE latent activation sets, and compares it with embedding-based MS. This is not the original individual-neuron image-response method.
record.method_sensitivity: The MS score depends on external encoder choice and its anisotropy; the paper reports a different score ordering under TMS. The text also reports differences in TMS/MS correlations across SAE configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: Embedding-based MS for SAE latents rises with the external encoder's anisotropy: CLIP highest, BLIP2 intermediate, DINOv3 lowest. This matches the anisotropy ranking (mean cosine 0.52/0.33/0.07).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Embedding-similarity monosemanticity scores of SAE latents are inflated by anisotropic encoders, so cross-model comparisons depend on encoder choice.

fits_no_version.finding: An activation-set coherence score (TMS) and MS mostly agree per latent, most strongly for DINOv3 (>0.75 in 16/18 configurations) and weakest for CLIP (down to 0.22). They give different model orderings and disagree on individual latents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Assessments of SAE-latent monosemanticity depend on the scoring metric, especially under anisotropic embedding spaces.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE-level mean TMS and MS correlate with probe-based concept-deletion target drop at small N. For CLIP, both become non-significant at N=16 and N=32.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How well SAE-level monosemanticity scores predict concept-deletion effectiveness depends on base model and deletion size.

record.code_released: The text states that code is in an anonymous Zenodo repository with a private review link to be made public on acceptance; URL not stated.
record.peer_reviewed: Preprint; the text says a shorter version was accepted for the post-workshop proceedings of the 8th International Workshop on eXplainable Knowledge Discovery in Data Mining (XKDD 2026).
record.problems: The study evaluates SAE latents, not the ordinary individual neurons at issue in the claim. Its TMS is an operational proxy for coherence, and the paper itself describes latents as concept proxies rather than ground-truth semantic concepts. The evaluation uses Mini-ImageNet and three pretrained feature sources. Some reported score results are available only in plots; the text does not give their exact values.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted to meet the 60-row limit. The paper's training-trajectory and within-activation-set variance results were not separately recorded because they do not directly test the claim versions beyond the score comparisons already recorded.

untested.parts: No individual neurons of image classifiers are examined; only SAE latents over DINOv3/CLIP/BLIP2 embeddings.
No language-model MLP neurons are examined.
Superposition is mentioned in related work only; not tested.
Varies SAE type, K and expansion factor, but scores SAE latents, not the share of polysemantic network neurons across architectures.
No network neurons are scored. Encoder- and metric-dependence is shown only for SAE latent monosemanticity scores. Activation-range dependence is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked r1–r10 to V7, but these rows score SAE dictionary latents, not network neurons. Most of them also compare the study's own metric with an alternative, which the rules exclude as version evidence. No verdicts are given. Tables 2 (variance correlations) and the training-dynamics figures are likewise method-validation results and need no rows.

versions.untested_parts: Individual neurons in image classifiers, including InceptionV1 neurons and their responses to unrelated images.
Transformer language-model MLP neurons and the prevalence of unrelated token or context responses.
Whether superposition or a feature-to-neuron capacity shortfall causes polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.

The share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization conditions, and whether it can be lowered without substantial performance loss. The study varies SAE configurations but does not measure that share.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons are actually detecting one shared feature or related offshoots rather than unrelated mixtures.
The study compares scoring measures and encoder choices, but does not vary which portion of a neuron's activation range is examined.

rows.problem: Ordering stated in text (DINOv3 lowest); plotted values not given.
Ordering stated in text (BLIP2 intermediate); plotted values not given.
Ordering stated in text (CLIP highest); plotted values not given.

relation.reason: The SAE approach it relies on is premised on polysemantic or entangled neurons, but it tests no version. The reader's earlier call of tests/T2 does not fit.

tranche.reason: The paper proposes a new coherence score (TMS) for SAE latents and uses neuron polysemanticity and superposition only as motivation. It reports only how its metric compares with MS and gives no rate or degree of polysemanticity in base-network neurons.

source_check.notes: The units scored are SAE latents ('latent neurons'), not base-network neurons. The encoder dependence of MS concerns score inflation from anisotropy, not whether a unit counts as polysemantic. Fig. 1b values are only in the figure. The text names the checkpoints dinov3-convnext-tiny, clip-vit-base-patch32 and blip2-opt-2.7b, though the row subjects give size as not stated.

statements.correction: Fig. 1a: sigma_cosine 0.52 (CLIP), 0.33 (BLIP2), 0.07 (DINOv3); PC1 EVR 0.07, 0.05, 0.02. Fig. 1b: MS over non-zero-MS neurons, TopK SAE, K=10, CLIP > BLIP2 > DINOv3.
statements.problem: Matches the text. Section 5 gives mean pairwise cosine (sigma_cosine) of 0.52 for CLIP, 0.33 for BLIP2 and 0.07 for DINOv3. It says MS is highest with CLIP, intermediate with BLIP2 and lowest with DINOv3, and that this ordering follows the anisotropy ranking. Fig. 1b is TopK K=10; the caption says 'across setups'.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Embedding-based MS across DINOv3, BLIP2, and CLIP encoders; comparison with TMS
reader_labels.reason: MS ordering follows encoder anisotropy, while TMS yields a different, more balanced ordering; TMS–MS correlations and qualitative examples also show that metric choice changes the assessment (r1–r10).
